content: Paederus dermatitis, also known as linear dermatitis or dermatitis linearis, is a skin condition caused by contact with the hemolymph of certain rove beetles, particularly those belonging to the genus Paederus. This condition is also referred to by various local names, such as spider-lick, whiplash dermatitis, and Nairobi fly dermatitis. The primary irritant responsible for this reaction is a toxin called pederin, although other similar molecules, such as pederone and pseudopederin, may also be involved depending on the beetle species. Occasionally, the term blister beetle dermatitis is incorrectly used to describe this condition, though it more accurately refers to dermatitis caused by cantharidin from blister beetles. When pederin comes into contact with the skin, it can spread to other areas of the skin, leading to secondary lesions. A characteristic feature of this condition is the appearance of kissing or mirror-image lesions, which occur when two skin surfaces come into contact, such as in the elbow flexure. Immediate washing of the affected skin with soap and water is strongly recommended if contact with a rove beetle is suspected. Initially, contact with pederin does not produce any visible reaction. However, within 12 to 36 hours, a reddish rash (erythema) develops, which subsequently progresses to blister formation. The irritation may persist for two to three weeks and can include crusting and scaling. A study has shown that the most effective treatment involves a combination of topical steroids, oral antihistamines, and antibiotics. The use of antibiotics is thought to be beneficial due to the potential contamination of the skin by pederin-producing bacteria. Several genera of rove beetles, all members of the subtribe Paederina, are known to cause Paederus dermatitis. These include Paederus, Paederidus, and Megalopaederus. The toxin pederin is highly toxic and is considered more potent than cobra venom. Different species of rove beetles are responsible for this condition in various parts of the world: Paederus melampus, also known as the Manipal bug or Nitte Police, is found in the Indian state of Karnataka. This species was identified in a 2007 study by dermatologists from Sri Devaraj Medical College in Karnataka. Despite being called blister beetles in some cases, rove beetles like P. melampus belong to the family Staphylinidae, which is distinct from the blister beetle family Meloidae. Paederus brasiliensis, also referred to as El podo, causes dermatitis in South America. Another species, Paederus columbinus, is found in Venezuela. Paederus fuscipes is a major cause of linear dermatitis in northern Iran, where it is an urban problem in provinces along the Caspian Sea shore, as opposed to being a rural issue in the south. This species also causes linear dermatitis in Taiwan. The Nairobi fly, which includes Paederus crebrepunctatus and Paederus sabaeus, is responsible for dermatitis in East Africa. Paederus dermatitis has also been reported in other regions, including Nigeria, France, Okinawa, Australia, Malaysia, and Sri Lanka.
